findings.title: The spatial and force interfaces force per-agent Python loops, contradicting the slice's own criterion and the architecture's hot-loop goal
findings.description:
Step 3 (line 88) has the tick call `SpatialQuery.query_radius(position, radius)` once per active agent. `BulkForce` then receives `neighbor_lists: list[NDArray]` and `profiles: list[BehavioralProfile]`. Both are ragged Python lists with one entry per agent.
- This is a Python-level per-agent loop in the hot path. It directly contradicts line 247 ("No Python-level per-agent loops in the hot path") and the architecture's Design Goal (arch:33).
- It also contradicts the architecture's GPU note (arch:99): "bulk array-in/array-out… no Python-level per-agent branching… no callbacks into Python."
- Arch:87 says the interface must let the strategy be replaced "without touching the force computation code." Slice 105 (spatial hash) and any GPU query would have to emit a per-agent call and ragged lists.
- `SpatialQuery`, `BulkForce` and `tick` are consumed by slices 101-105. Changing them later is a breaking change across every behavior slice. The shape must be fixed now.
- Suggested fix: use a batch query, `query_radius_batch(positions, radii)`, that returns a flat CSR-style `(offsets, indices)` pair. Pass the same structure to `BulkForce`, and pass profile parameters as per-agent arrays.

findings.title: `BulkForce` contract is ambiguous about alignment and return shape, and the "full-population N×2" return contradicts the subset semantics
findings.description:
- Line 152 says integration adds force to velocity "for all, but only active agents have non-zero forces." Line 91 and line 215 say inactive state is untouched, and that integration applies only to active agents.
  - If position is advanced for all agents, inactive agents move whenever they have nonzero velocity.
  - A velocity clamp applied to all agents also modifies inactive velocities.
  - Only one reading can be correct, and the design states both.
- The design doesn't say whether `neighbor_lists[k]` belongs to agent `active_indices[k]` or to agent `k`. When `active_indices=None`, the two readings coincide, so tests with the default wouldn't catch the difference.
- It also doesn't say whether `profiles` is the profile table (indexed by `profile_indices`) or a per-agent list. The tick signature (line 182) uses the former sense.
- Returning an N×2 array for a 3-of-100 subset allocates O(N) per force per tick. That undercuts the scaling story, where a small active subset of a large population is the point. It also conflicts with the "no dynamic allocation" GPU note (arch:99).
- Suggested fix: return `len(active)×2`, aligned with `active_indices`, and have integration scatter it.

findings.title: `Force` (per-agent) protocol has no path through `tick()`
findings.description:
- `tick()` accepts `forces: list[BulkForce]` only. Line 152 says "the tick loop prefers the bulk variant when available", but nothing in the design selects between the two or adapts a `Force` to a `BulkForce`.
- The criterion at line 248 says placeholder forces "exercise both protocol paths". No `Force` path exists in `tick`.
- Per-agent `Force` is not in the architecture or the slice plan entry; the architecture mentions only the BulkForce pattern (arch:99). It adds a second protocol and a placeholder force whose only purpose is to be tested.
- Either cut it. Or keep it as a test-side reference oracle, with a small adapter that checks `BulkForce` output against the per-agent result, and say that explicitly.

findings.title: BruteForceQuery description is internally inconsistent and hides an O(N²) memory cost
findings.description:
- Line 173 says `build()` "computes all pairwise distances" and `query_radius()` filters. But `query_radius` takes an arbitrary `position` and a `radius`, not an agent index, so a precomputed pairwise matrix can't answer it.
- Taken literally, an N×N float64 matrix is 800 MB at 10K agents. The architecture's target is "tens of thousands" (arch:33). Query cost would also still be O(N) per call, so O(N²) in total per tick on top of the build.
- `build()` should store (copy) the positions. The design doesn't say whether it keeps a reference or a copy. Integration mutates `state.positions` in place, so a stored reference would see mutated data.
- The query contract also leaves these open:
  - Whether the querying agent itself is included in the result.
  - Whether the radius test is `<` or `<=`.
  - The ordering of returned indices. Ascending order is needed for deterministic force summation order and therefore bit-exact determinism.
  - Behavior for `radius <= 0`.

findings.title: Parent-architecture scale NFR is neither restated nor reconciled with the slice's "hundreds of agents" target
findings.description:
- The architecture sets "tens of thousands of agents at full fidelity on a single CPU process" (arch:33), and the tick/neighbor path touches that.
- The slice never restates this. Line 173 quietly lowers the target to "hundreds of agents".
- No success criterion or test states what population the slice's implementation is verified at. Nothing says that BruteForceQuery is expected to miss the architecture target until slice 105.
- Add a stated target, or an explicit deferral to 105 with the verified scale for this slice.

findings.title: `tick()` return contract diverges from the plan and architecture
findings.description:
- Line 39 says the tick will "return updated state". The signature at line 187 is `-> None`, mutating in place.
- The architecture step 5 says "Returns the updated state array" (arch:67) and "feed in state, get back state" (arch:70). The slice plan says "agents that move under applied forces… deterministic output."
- The in-place choice may be fine, but it must be stated as a decision and the "return" wording removed. As written, consumers can't tell which contract holds.

findings.title: Subset-evaluation invariants are not testable as written, and `active_indices` handling is unspecified
findings.description:
- Walkthrough step 5 verifies agent 0 "can still find agent 50" by querying the spatial object directly. That doesn't prove `tick()` builds from the full population, which is the criterion at line 242.
- The placeholder forces ignore neighbors. Nothing observable in `tick` exposes the neighbor lists. The design needs a spy `SpatialQuery` that records the `build()` argument, and a recording force that captures `neighbor_lists`.
- `active_indices` input handling is unspecified, and the project guideline is to fail explicitly. Cases to cover:
  - An empty `np.array([])` has dtype float64 and raises on fancy indexing.
  - Duplicate indices.
  - Out-of-range indices.
  - A boolean mask. The plan and architecture say "index array or mask" (arch:49, plan:17), but the design silently supports indices only.
  - Duplicates with `+=` fancy indexing apply once, which is a silent semantic.

findings.title: `accelerations` array and the force-to-velocity unit are unspecified
findings.description:
- `accelerations` is part of `AgentState` (line 96) but is never read or written by the tick or by integration. Integration uses `velocity += force*dt` directly.
- The architecture lists only positions, velocities and profile indices (arch:39). This is state with no consumer and no stated owner.
- Mass is also implicitly 1, so force equals acceleration. This is never stated, and slices 101-104 will depend on that unit.
- Either cut `accelerations`, or define who writes it and what it holds.

findings.title: Integration semantics under-specified and the verification math is off
findings.description:
- "Clamp to `max_speed`" doesn't say whether it is a norm clamp (rescale the vector) or a per-component clamp. Test results differ.
- Line 90 lists the clamp after the position update. The section at lines 208-213 puts it before. One of the two is wrong.
- Per-agent `max_speed` must be gathered from a `list[BehavioralProfile]` via `profile_indices`. The design doesn't say how this is vectorized. A list comprehension over dataclass objects is a per-agent Python loop, which again contradicts line 247. A parameter table or array form is needed.
- Walkthrough step 4 expects displacement "proportional to t²". Semi-implicit Euler gives x_n = a·dt²·n(n+1)/2, not exactly t². The test must say so and set tolerances.
- The clamp also breaks the parabola once speed reaches `max_speed`. The example profile has `max_speed=5.0`, so the test parameters must stay under it.

findings.title: Agent add/remove semantics break caller-held indices
findings.description:
- Arch:81 requires "register/remove agents" and the world server holds `active_indices` across ticks. The design gives no signatures for add/remove.
- It doesn't say whether removal shifts indices (invalidating callers' `active_indices`) or swap-removes. It doesn't say whether there is a stable agent id, or what is returned on add. The world server needs a stable mapping from its entities to engine rows.
- Per-agent array resize through repeated append is also O(N) per add. For bulk spawning of tens of thousands of agents that is O(N²).
- State the index-stability contract and the bulk-add path.

findings.title: Verification walkthrough steps cannot run as written
findings.description:
- Step 3 uses `forces=[...]` and has no `import numpy as np`.
- The placeholder forces (`ConstantDrift`, `VelocityDrag`) are never named or given constructor signatures in this document. The names appear only in the tasks file.
- `AgentState.create(n=100, profiles=[profile])` has no specified signature. It doesn't say how initial positions are set. If they are zeros, 100 agents at one point is a degenerate determinism check. If they are random, a seed is needed.
- The shared `spatial` instance is reused across two states. This works only because `build` is called each tick, but it is not called out.
- `cd migratory` then `pip install -e ".[dev]"` implies a nested `migratory/` directory. The repo root already holds `project-documents/`, and the component tree at line 56 is ambiguous about whether `pyproject.toml` is at repo root or in a nested folder.
- State the dev extras and `requires-python` in the document, rather than only in the tasks file.

findings.title: `DIMS` "single-point change" claim is overstated, and the constant has no stated home
findings.description:
- The slice plan and architecture don't ask for 3D. `DIMS` is an abstraction nothing uses yet.
- The claim of a "single-point change" is false as written:
  - The `Force` docstring says "2D force vector".
  - The `BulkForce` return type is "N×2".
  - Placeholder force vectors and test fixtures will hardcode 2-vectors.
  - Tests assert N×2 shapes.
- The constant isn't in the component tree, and the module that would hold it is not stated. It would be shared by `engine` and `spatial` through the root package.
- Either drop the claim and keep `DIMS` as a convenience, or defer it. If kept, name its module.

findings.title: Environment input surface is silently deferred
findings.description: Arch:63 and arch:47 list environmental context as a tick input. The tick signature has none, and the Excluded list doesn't mention it. The statement at line 225 that "behavioral slices add forces; they don't modify the tick loop" will not hold once the Environment Layer arrives. Record the deferral explicitly. A `**context` or optional parameter could be added later without breaking callers.

findings.title: Per-call `dt` limits variable-rate ticking, and the `tick()` docs don't say how callers should use it
findings.description: Variable-rate ticking at 1/4 or 1/16 rate needs a larger `dt` for slow groups. With a single scalar `dt`, the caller must call `tick()` once per rate group. Each call rebuilds the full spatial index and sees positions already mutated by earlier groups, so results depend on call order. This is a world-server decision, but the docs should state the contract (a single `dt` per call, and an order-dependence warning).

findings.title: Document formatting defect: the integration section renders as a code block
findings.description: The `### Integration: Semi-Implicit Euler` heading and its body are indented four spaces. In Markdown that renders as a literal code block, not a section. Dedent it.
